title: The studio desk
scenario:
Your agency built a chat assistant for client work. It has three tools, listed in the exhibit. The exhibit also has a chat log from a test.

The tool list and the log are made up for this case. They follow the tool-calling pattern in the vendors' docs. Read the log before you answer.

The client's brief says 16:9, but nobody typed it in the chat.
exhibit:
Tools (our own example for this case)
  make_image       "Makes an image."
                   inputs: prompt, aspect_ratio (required)
  edit_image       "Edits the image the user is looking at."
                   inputs: instruction
  post_to_social   "Posts the current image to the brand's account."
                   inputs: caption

Chat log (made up for this case)
  user:      Make a banner for the autumn sale.
  assistant: [calls make_image(prompt="autumn sale banner")]
  note:      tool run rejected: aspect_ratio missing
  assistant: [calls make_image(prompt="autumn sale banner", aspect_ratio="1:1")]
  user:      Nice. Make the sky bluer.
  assistant: [calls make_image(prompt="autumn sale banner, bluer sky",
                               aspect_ratio="1:1")]
  user:      Great, post it.
  assistant: [calls post_to_social(caption="Autumn sale!")]

questions.prompt: The brief said 16:9, but the chat never said it. The banner came back 1:1. Which design fix is the best?

options.text: Tell the client to always write a longer first message.
options.explanation: A short request is normal. The tool design should handle a missing value, not the client.

options.text: Remove the aspect_ratio input so the tool never needs it.
options.explanation: The tool needs a shape to make the image. Removing the input hides the choice instead of making it right.

options.text: Say in the make_image description that aspect_ratio must come from the user. Make the assistant ask when it is missing.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's docs show a model can guess a missing required value, and say this is not guaranteed. Here the assistant filled in 1:1 itself. Fix it in the tool description or the chat flow.

options.text: Accept it. The model always picks the best ratio.
options.explanation: The model guessed 1:1. Anthropic's docs say it may guess values you didn't supply.

questions.prompt: "Make the sky bluer" made a brand new image instead of changing the approved one. What is the best change?

options.text: Nothing can be done. The model decides and that is final.
options.explanation: Anthropic's docs say you can set tool_choice to require a tool call. OpenAI's image tool has an action setting for forcing edit or generate.

options.text: Add five more tools so the assistant has more choices.
options.explanation: More tools do not clear up a confusing pair. Google's tips also cap the active set at 10-20 tools.

options.text: Switch to a bigger model and the problem will vanish.
options.explanation: No doc promises that. Tool choice depends on the descriptions and settings you give.

options.text: Make the descriptions say that make_image creates a new image and edit_image changes the current one. Add a rule for when to use each.
options.explanation: Right. The model picks a tool from its name and description. Google's best practices say to be clear and specific. Anthropic (`tool_choice`) and OpenAI (the image tool's `action`) also let you force the choice.

questions.prompt: Which tool should have a person approve each call?

options.text: None. The model checks its own requests before acting.
options.explanation: A tool call is the model's request, not a check. Google lists validating calls before executing them as a best practice.

options.text: make_image
options.explanation: It only makes a draft. A wrong call costs a little time.

options.text: post_to_social
options.explanation: Right. It has an outside effect: it reaches the brand's audience. This is our rule for send tools. Google also lists validating calls before executing them.

options.text: edit_image
options.explanation: It also only changes a draft. A wrong call can be undone by editing again.

questions.prompt: In the log, who ran make_image?

options.text: The model, inside itself, while it was writing the reply.
options.explanation: Google's docs say the model does not execute the function itself.

options.text: Nobody. A tool call is only a label in the log.
options.explanation: A tool call is a real request. The docs show a result that is sent back to the model.

options.text: Something outside the model: your application, or a vendor's built-in tool. The model only asked for it.
options.explanation: Right. Google says the model does not execute the function itself. Anthropic and OpenAI describe the same loop: the model returns a call, and an application or built-in tool runs it.

options.text: The user's browser, because the user typed the request.
options.explanation: The docs say an application executes client tools, or the vendor runs server or built-in tools. Nothing says the user's browser runs them.

questions.prompt: The agency adds twelve more tools with long descriptions. What happens to the cost of each chat turn?

options.text: It goes up. Anthropic says tool names, descriptions and schemas count as input tokens.
options.explanation: Right. Tool definitions are sent with the request, so they add input tokens even on turns that call no tool.

options.text: It goes down, because the model has more ready-made answers.
options.explanation: Nothing in the docs says extra tools lower cost.

options.text: It stays the same. Tool definitions are free.
options.explanation: Anthropic's docs list the tools parameter as a source of extra input tokens.

options.text: It only changes on turns where a tool is called.
options.explanation: Tool definitions are sent with each request that includes them, whether or not a tool is called.
